title: 'Disgraceful': India's Umpire Pressure Sparks Storm After Narrow Japan T20 Win
excerpt: A reversed wide call in the final over at Sano has drawn accusations that Indian players bullied the umpires — overshadowing a two-run win meant to celebrate 75 years of India-Japan ties.
body:
• India's two-run T20I win over Japan in Sano has been overshadowed by accusations that Indian players pressured umpires into reversing a wide call in the final over.
  • With Japan needing six runs off four balls, captain Shreyas Iyer and bowler Axar Patel confronted the officials after a wide was signalled — the decision was overturned after consultation.
  • Cricket's Law 2.12 allows an umpire to alter a decision, but the incident has reignited debate over dissent, with critics calling India's conduct "disgraceful."
  • The match, played to mark 75 years of India-Japan diplomatic ties, was India's final warm-up before its Asian Games campaign begins on September 28.

India survived a mighty scare against Japan in Sano on Tuesday, winning a rain-shortened one-off T20I by two runs. But the result — India's 200th win in the format — has been almost entirely eclipsed by what happened in the final over: a wide call, an on-field confrontation, and a reversed decision that has drawn accusations of umpire intimidation from across the cricket world.

What happened in the final over

The contest, reduced to five overs a side by rain, came down to the last over with Japan needing six runs off four balls — within sight of arguably the greatest upset in international cricket history. Axar Patel was bowling to Japan's Alexander Shirai-Patmore, who attempted a reverse sweep and missed. Umpire Chris Thurgate, standing in his 18th T20I, signalled wide.

The reaction was immediate. Axar and wicketkeeper Sanju Samson protested, and captain Shreyas Iyer walked across to the square-leg umpire, Chris Brown of New Zealand — a member of the ICC's Elite Panel — to demand intervention. After a consultation between the two officials, Thurgate reversed his call. The delivery was ruled legal, Japan's equation stiffened, and India closed out a two-run win.

There was no television umpire at the match and no Decision Review System in operation, leaving the on-field officials as the final authority — and their reversed decision as the talking point of the night.

What the laws actually say

On the narrow question of whether an umpire can change a call, the laws are clear. Law 2.12 of cricket's laws states that "an umpire may alter any decision provided that such alteration is made promptly," with limited exceptions around dead-ball rulings. On that basis, the reversal itself was within the umpires' powers.

The wider question is whether India's players crossed the line in how the reversal was obtained. Article 2.8 of the ICC's code of conduct covers "excessive, obvious disappointment with an umpire's decision" and "arguing or entering into a prolonged discussion with the umpire about his decision" — provisions that carry fines and suspension points at international level.

"With five off four needed for the biggest upset in cricket history, India have just bullied the umpires into overturning a wide call against Japan. Genuinely disgraceful."

— Ben Gardner, Wisden editor, on X

The backlash

The condemnation was swift. Wisden editor Ben Gardner wrote on X that India had "bullied the umpires into overturning a wide call," calling it "genuinely disgraceful." Former player and commentator Kartik Kannan argued the original wide call was incorrect but criticised India's conduct: "What's the point of being a cricket power if you can't use dissent to get your way," he wrote, adding that India was "unsporting in not respecting a decision, which they might have accepted if the stakes weren't so high."

Code Sports chief cricket writer Daniel Cherny focused on the precedent: "It's almost immaterial whether it was a wide or not. The game falls apart if an umpire's decision can be overturned following aggressive gesticulation from a player." Al Jazeera and Fox Sports Australia both led with the bullying allegation, ensuring the story travelled well beyond the subcontinent.

"It really was not a wide and finally the correct decision was taken, but the Indian team brought out their bully mode to make sure they weren't going to lose on account of a wrong decision."

— Kartik Kannan, on X

Why it matters beyond Sano

The irony is hard to miss: the fixture was staged to celebrate 75 years of diplomatic relations between India and Japan and to serve as a warm-up for the Asian Games, where India begins its cricket campaign on September 28. Instead of a feel-good occasion, the build-up to a major tournament is now dominated by a debate about sportsmanship.

For the ICC, the incident lands awkwardly. With no DRS at the match, the entire episode rested on two on-field umpires — one of whom, Thurgate, was officiating his home associate nation against the sport's financial superpower. Whether the governing body acts under its dissent provisions will be watched closely; silence would itself send a message about where the line sits.
image_caption: India's Axar Patel speaks with the umpire during the T20I against Japan in Sano. A wide call off Patel's bowling in the final over was reversed after Indian players confronted the officials, drawing accusations of umpire intimidation.
nri_angle: Indian cricket fans abroad are split between relief at the win and unease at the conduct, as the episode puts sportsmanship — not cricket — at the centre of India's Asian Games build-up.
author: Diaspora Desk
